blogs.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
blogs.title: Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive
blogs.description: After two days of experience with Claude Fable 5 I think the best way to describe it is relentlessly proactive. It knows a whole lot of…
blogs.content:
After two days of experience with Claude Fable 5 I think the best way to describe it is relentlessly proactive . It knows a whole lot of tricks and it will deploy pretty much any of them to get to its goal.

 I'll illustrate this with an example. I was hacking on Datasette Agent today when I noticed a glitch: a horizontal scrollbar that shouldn't be there in the jump menu chat prompt. I snapped this screenshot:

 Then I started a fresh claude session in my datasette-agent checkout, dragged in the screenshot and told it:

 Look at dependencies to help figure out why there is a horizontal scrollbar here

 I had a hunch the cause was in a dependency of Datasette Agent (likely Datasette itself) and I knew Fable was good at digging into dependency code, either by inspecting installed files in its own virtual environment site-packages or by referencing a local checkout on disk. Telling it to start with dependencies felt like a good bet.

 I got distracted by a domestic task and wandered away from my computer.

 When I came back a few minutes later I saw my machine open a browser window in my regular Firefox and then navigate to the dialog in question . I had not told Claude Code to use any browser automation, and I was pretty sure it wasn't possible for it to trigger mouse movements or keyboard shortcuts within a window, so how was it doing that?

 I watched in fascination as it continued with its explorations, then saw it open a Safari window instead of Firefox. I also grabbed this snapshot from the Claude terminal:

 What was it doing there with uv run --with pyobjc-framework-Quartz ?

 It turns out Fable had hacked up its own pattern for taking screenshots of browser windows. It was using Python to iterate through all available windows on my machine, then filtering for Safari windows with expected strings such as "textarea" in the window name. It used that to find their window number - an integer like 153551 - which it could then use with the screencapture CLI tool to grab a PNG.

 OK fine, that's a neat way of taking screenshots. But what was it taking screenshots of?

 Turns out it had been writing its own scratch HTML pages to try and recreate the bug, then opening Safari and grabbing screenshots.

 Here's that /tmp/textarea-scrollbar-test.html page it created, and the screenshot it took with screencapture -x -o -l 153551 /tmp/safari-cases.png :

(I have way too many open tabs!)

 OK, so I can see how it's opening test pages and taking screenshots, but how on earth was it triggering the modal dialog that was meant to be under test? That's only available via a click or a keyboard shortcut, and I couldn't see a mechanism for it to run those in Safari.

 I eventually figured out what it had done.

 Claude was running in a folder that contained the source code for the application. It knows enough about Datasette to be able to run a local development server. It turns out it was editing Datasette's own templates to add JavaScript that would trigger the correct keyboard shortcut as soon as the window opened, adding code like this:

 script >
 window . addEventListener ( "load" , function ( ) {
 setTimeout ( function ( ) {
 document . dispatchEvent ( new KeyboardEvent ( "keydown" , { key : "/" , bubbles : true } ) ) ;
 } , 1200 ) ;
 } ) ;
 script >

 1.2 seconds after the window opens, this code triggers a simulated / key, which is the keyboard shortcut for opening the modal dialog.

 There was one challenge left. In order to understand what was going on, Claude needed to run JavaScript on the page to take measurements for itself.

 It wrote its own custom web application to capture information via CORS, then ran that as a local server and opened a page with JavaScript that would POST directly to it!

 Here's the Python web app it wrote, using the standard library http.server package:

 from http . server import HTTPServer , BaseHTTPRequestHandler

 class H ( BaseHTTPRequestHandler ):
 def do_POST ( self ):
 n = int ( self . headers . get ( "Content-Length" , 0 ))
 open ( "/tmp/diag.json" , "w" ). write ( self . rfile . read ( n ). decode ())
 self . send_response ( 200 )
 self . send_header ( "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" , "*" )
 self . end_headers ()
 def do_OPTIONS ( self ):
 self . send_response ( 200 )
 self . send_header ( "Access-Control-Allow-Origin" , "*" )
 self . send_header ( "Access-Control-Allow-Headers" , "*" )
 self . end_headers ()
 def log_message ( self , * a ): # quiet
 pass

 HTTPServer (( "127.0.0.1" , 9999 ), H ). serve_forever ()
 All this does is accept a POST request full of JSON and write that to the /tmp/diag.json file. It sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * headers (including from OPTIONS requests) so that code running on another domain can still communicate back to it.

 Then Claude injected this code into the template that it was loading in a browser:

 const host = document . querySelector ( "navigation-search" ) ;
 const ta = host . shadowRoot . querySelector ( "textarea" ) ;
 const cs = getComputedStyle ( ta ) ;
 fetch ( "http://127.0.0.1:9999/diag" , {
 method : "POST" ,
 body : JSON . stringify ( {
 dpr : window . devicePixelRatio ,
 scrollWidth : ta . scrollWidth , clientWidth : ta . clientWidth ,
 whiteSpace : cs . whiteSpace , width : cs . width ,
 } ) ,
 } ) ;

 This took measurements of the inside the Web Component and sent them to the server, which wrote them to a file on disk, which Claude could then read.

 Having figured out all of these tricks Fable... hit some invisible guardrail and downgraded itself to Opus. Thankfully Opus had access to the full transcript and could continue using the tricks pioneered by Fable, and shortly afterwards found, tested and verified the fix .

 I prompted Opus to:

 Write a report in /tmp/automation-report.md where you note down all of the tricks you have used in this session to test against real browsers on my computer, include runnable code examples

 Which produced this report , which was invaluable for piecing together the details of what had happened for this post.

 I've shared the full terminal transcript of the Claude Code session as well.

 A review of everything it did

 Based on a screenshot and a one-line prompt, Claude Fable 5 + Claude Code:

 Figured out the recipe to run the local development server (with fake environment variables needed to get it running)

 Fired up a Playwright Chrome session

 Turned on the visible scrollbars setting for Chrome defaults write com.google.chrome.for.testing AppleShowScrollBars Always (it turned that off again later)

 Cycled through Firefox and WebKit in Playwright too, failing to recreate the bug

 Worked out my default browser was Safari

 Built a textarea-scrollbar-test.html HTML document

 Opened that in real (not Playwright) Firefox

 Found that osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to tell process "firefox" to id of window 1' was blocked because "osascript is not allowed assistive access"

 Figured out that uv run --with pyobjc-framework-Quartz python workaround, described above

 Added JavaScript to the site templates in order to trigger the / key

 Built its own little Python CORS web server to capture JSON data

 Rewrote the template to capture that data and send it to the server

 Scripted its way through the Web Component shadow DOM to the information it needed

 Modified its custom template to hack in a potential fix

 Confirmed the hacked fix worked

 Reported back on how to fix the problem

 Like I said, relentlessly proactive!

 I really need to lock this thing down

 On the one hand, watching Fable go to extreme lengths to get the information that it needed to debug what was, in the end, a two-line CSS fix, was fascinating .

 But on the other hand... this is a robust reminder that coding agents can do anything you can do by typing commands into a terminal - and frontier models know every trick in the book and evidently a few that nobody has ever written down before.

 If Fable had been acting on malicious instructions - a prompt injection attack hidden in code or an issue thread, or something I'd carelessly pasted into my terminal - it's alarming to think quite how far it could go to exfiltrate data or cause other forms of mischief.

 Running coding agents outside of a sandbox has always been a bad idea - it's my top contendor for a Challenger disaster incident, as described by Johann Rehberger in The Normalization of Deviance in AI .

 Fable is arguably smarter and hence more suspicious of potentially malicious instructions. But that smartness is very much a two-edged sword: if it does get subverted by instructions, the amount of damage it can do given its relentless proactivity is terrifying.

 Tags: ai , prompt-injection , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-programming , coding-agents , claude-code , claude-mythos

blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: An interview with Ben Bajarin about WWDC and the status of the AI compute industry.
blogs.content:
An interview with Ben Bajarin about WWDC and the status of the AI compute industry.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Ben Bajarin . Bajarin is the CEO and Principal Analyst for Creative Strategies , one of the oldest technology-focused market research firms. Bajarin and Creative Strategies have a particular focus on semiconductors, and Bajarin also hosts The Circuit Podcast about the semiconductor industry with previous Stratechery Interview subject Jay Goldberg. Recently Creative Strategies launched a new Substack called The Diligence Stack , featuring original market research and industry analysis. I previously spoke with Bajarin in September 2024 and October 2025 .

In this interview we discuss WWDC and Apple’s AI announcements. We talk about what they launched, not just in terms of AI, but also why the company was focused on improving the underlying platform. We also discuss their architectural choices, including on-device inference and using Nvidia chips on Google’s Cloud. After that we discuss AI compute broadly, including Nvidia’s new PC chip, Vera, CPUs and agents, and Intel’s change in fortunes. And, at the end, we talk about Creative Strategies’ new offering.

As a reminder, all Stratechery content, including interviews, is available as a podcast; click the link at the top of this email to add Stratechery to your podcast player.

On to the Interview:

An Interview with Ben Bajarin About Apple, AI, and Compute

This interview is lightly edited for clarity.

Topics:

WWDC Foundations | Consumer vs. Enterprise AI | Apple’s AI Architecture | Project Solara | The Nvidia PC | CPUs in the Data Center | Compute Capacity | CPUs in the Data Center | The Diligence Stack

WWDC Foundations

Ben Bajarin, welcome back to Stratechery.

BB: Hello, Ben Thompson. Thanks for having me again.

I’ve been wanting to have you back on for a while, and we finally got a good occasion this week, which is WWDC , so let’s start there. What was your overall take on the keynote, beyond it being shockingly short?

BB: Shockingly short, which I thought was interesting, because any of us who’ve watched this for a while know WWDC used to be a product or vertical operating system set of narratives — here’s macOS, here’s iPadOS, here’s whatever. This was a platform conversation, and so I thought that was different.

My read on that — and I don’t think this was my overall take coming into this, but the realization afterwards — is that to do all the things we want them to succeed in or do with generative AI, and AI in a smart Siri, a lot needed to be re-architected at the platform level.

And by platform, do you mean not just at the operating system level, but Apple as a platform broadly?

BB: Correct. Every platform essentially needed to be re-architected, you probably felt this too — we have a lot of conversations, and they’re always like, “You know what, operating systems and platforms just get crusty, they’re old, they’ve been built on something that was great 10 years ago and not now”. This is the same problem that Microsoft’s been trying to go through with Windows to modernize it, a lot just needs to be modernized, and that’s hard to do when you’ve got billions of customers.

So that I thought was the take of, “We need to do these things” — when’s the last time Apple’s mentioned a CPU scheduler? They update CPU schedulers all the time — they just felt the need to call out that they’ve actually done it even more, and the index, when’s the last time they talked about, “Hey, we rebuilt the index”? That’s boring on the surface, but necessary to do all this stuff with Siri and Apple Intelligence.

I thought the index was a really notable point, because if you understood broadly what the point of Siri was, it was notable that they spent so much time on the index. This was my overall take on the AI story, they’re perfecting a 2024 AI story, which is when they announced Apple Intelligence . This was basically, “Let’s do what we said in 2024, but for real this time”. To what extent was there the realization that the reason why Siri failed wasn’t just because the models were bad or whatever it might be, but because if we’re going to do RAG , we actually have to have a functional search index, and they didn’t have that”?

BB: I think it’s related — that’s exactly right. Obviously, we wanted them to get here sooner — I don’t think any of us perhaps appreciated the magnitude of the platform re-architecture that was needed to do this.

What about us? What about Apple?

BB: Well, that’s the thing. The broader question would be, “Could you have done some of this sooner? Is it all necessary?” — maybe that’s the case, but the reality is, and you’re exactly right, I would imagine that search, and semantic search, and better contextual search, is actually going to be one of the things that people do a lot of, and so having the index get redone was a key part of being able to do that. Maybe it wouldn’t have worked before.

Well, all the Siri demos that are super obviously useful, and that, from what I’ve seen, seem to clearly work, are basically just fancy search at the end of the day. Is that a fair characterization?

BB: Correct, yes, absolutely. And again, that’s one of the things where that’s been like a black hole for a lot of people — you lose a lot of stuff, you’re not organized.

And also, if you ever tried to search in Messages, you realize that — I mean, that was almost like a tell, right?

BB: It doesn’t work at all.

If you go back to the “When does my mom land in San Francisco?” demo, which was never actually demoed, but just talked about in 2024, you realize I can’t actually find a message from my mom in iMessage today.

BB: Ever!

So on what aspect is Siri going to be able to find it?

BB: Yeah, 100%. Or I could say, “Search for something from Ben Thompson”, and you don’t show up at all. And I was like, “He’s in my contacts, how can you not find this message?”, it’s just stuff that now, in a gen AI world, you’d walk back and say, “If it didn’t do those things, I would view it as a failure”, and so it needs to do those things, and that’s why the platform needs to be updated.

So broad picture, taking a platform approach was kind of what they did, because all those pillars led up to now trying to mainstream generative AI and bring it to the masses — they had to do those first two things first.

Do you think that is enough? Is actually just being, “State of the art in 2024 but it actually works, and you happen to own the operating system and have all that data” — do customers actually want anything more than that ?

BB: I think there’s a base level of expectation that my device does these things, and I think that’s where they landed. If you just look at even Gemini — Gemini is fine, it’s definitely not OpenAI or Claude in terms of its capabilities yet, it does what you need it to do when you’re searching and might want to interact with your calendar. These are basic things, and I also step back and say most consumers on the long tail of adoption are not using this for anything more than search. When they use GPT or Claude, it’s just search.

The two big use cases that I seem to see for normal people are recipes and do-it-yourself projects, which are fancy search at the end of the day.

BB: Yes, fancy search. So that’s why I think the interesting part here is, if we know that a lot of people kind of don’t do these things other than search — most people are not doing full workflow automation for their lives — they might do this for some work stuff, but they’re not doing it for their lives. That connecting to a consumer job, or the agent that I hire to go make a change in my calendar or find this image or have deeper semantic search — these are still new behaviors, and having a way that Apple mainstreams that in a way everybody can use it, for me, was always the key. Could they do it in a way that even grandma can use and find useful? That I just don’t think was an easy mountain to climb, and it looks like what they’ve got has gotten to a point where, honestly, it doesn’t always even mean you need to use Siri — it will be invisible in the background, but still be useful.

So this useful AI in an application, or applied AI, which is kind of the term I was using — if you just use robotics and applied robotics as a term, it moves from the lab to the mainstream — this is applied AI at a consumer level, and I think they got to that point and honestly, that’s all people will need. If they want to go off and do advanced other workflow stuff, there’s other models, and that’s totally fine.

When do you think Apple realized they needed to have their own — because they tried to draw this clear line between world knowledge and personal knowledge in 2024 — when did they realize that actually this is a line that does not make sense at all?

BB: I think for them — and we’ve talked about this too — there needs to be value in general search. The assumption when I heard, “Hey, we might be working with Gemini”, or when the rumor was out, was, “Oh cool, search is going to get good, because I use this on my device a lot”. So the idea is that they are bringing what they’re calling Apple world knowledge to this, and to some degree it sounds like it’s their index — they’re trying to separate themselves from Google. But that’s a core function that’s necessary, and to be honest with you, that’s a core function that’s necessary if we assume that they want to do glasses someday, and you might ask it about not just your food, but a flower or a bird or whatnot. So it needs to have that broad world knowledge, as they call it, and be something that they own and maintain.

Consumer vs. Enterprise AI

Do you think consumers will ever care about agents and things like that?

BB: No, I don’t. This is actually something I want to talk to you about.

Oh, I’m getting interviewed now.

BB: Yes! You and I were both born in the era of disruption theory and Jobs to Be Done . Is this not one of the most cleanly interesting examples? I’m hiring something, I don’t need to think it’s an agent, but I’m hiring something, in this case it’s Siri, or is it GPT, or is it Anthropic, to go do something for me to get jobs done, and how I disintermediate what those jobs are. Is it summarize an email? Is it do this for my calendar? This to me is a super interesting jobs to be done, in its purest definition, of, “Why would I choose this control plane layer?”. Don’t even think agent — just think something I interact with, and it goes and does this stuff for me. Consumer jobs, enterprise jobs, whatever it is, this is purely jobs to be done competition in the mental model. It doesn’t have to be an agent, it’s just I use this one thing and it can go do these things for me, because it has system-level access, app-level access, Internet-level access, all of those things.

My view on this has gotten quite coarse, which is, enterprises want to do work , they want their employees to be productive, because they’re paying the employees, they want to get more bang for their dollar, or perhaps replace those employees with something that is at least theoretically cheaper. Consumers don’t want to do work! The whole point of being a consumer is you don’t want to be at work, you want to be entertained, and in that context, I’m just broadly skeptical.

Again, as I put in my Article this week , I think this is a lesson that tech has had to relearn every decade or so. OpenAI is like the modern Dropbox — sort of timely with Drew Houston stepping down these days. Remember Dropbox, they wanted to be a consumer company so bad, even after it was clear their only market was enterprise, they launched that Carousel product, this beautiful photos thing, and I remember I wrote at the time that Houston was so clearly so much more enthusiastic and passionate about this product — which they then killed a year later —...
